Hatchlings of Audouin's gull emerge from eggs that weigh between 84 and 92 grams, a substantial investment reflecting the demands of embryonic development in a warm Mediterranean climate. Newly hatched chicks typically have a wet body mass of approximately 40 grams [Wwb = approximately 40 grams], a value that underscores their semi-precocial developmental mode. The incubation period itself averages 28.5 days [ab = 28.5 days] under optimal artificial incubation conditions set at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature regime that mirrors the consistent warmth provided by attentive parents on the nest. This duration is notably longer than that reported for some smaller Laridae, likely linked to the relatively large egg size and the energetic constraints imposed by the species' coastal foraging ecology, where prey availability can be unpredictable. The careful thermoregulation of the egg is critical, as even minor deviations from this optimal temperature can delay hatching or compromise chick viability at emergence. Comparable incubation periods are observed in other large gulls of the genus Larus, reinforcing the relationship between egg mass and developmental timing within this lineage.

Once hatched, the nestling chick enters a period of rapid somatic growth, fueled by the residual yolk reserves and intensive biparental provisioning. The ultimate adult body mass of this species is estimated at approximately 770 grams [Wwi = approximately 770 grams] for a fully grown, nesting individual, although some asymptotic measurements of breeding adults have been recorded at around 660 grams. This body size places Audouin's gull at an intermediate position among Mediterranean gulls, being larger than the slender-billed gull but somewhat smaller than the yellow-legged gull. The energetic demands of achieving this mass are considerable, requiring a long period of postnatal development. Under the core body temperature typical of an active, homeothermic adult (40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]), the next major developmental milestone is fledging. Young gulls achieve their first sustained flight at an average of 29 days after hatching [tx = 29 days after hatching], a timing that reflects a trade-off between the need to avoid terrestrial predators and the time required for full feather maturation at a temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This fledgling age is consistent with that of other medium-sized larids breeding in similar coastal habitats.

The onset of gonadal maturation in Audouin's gull is a relatively rapid process compared to other life-history events. Young birds typically reach puberty at 87 days after hatching [tp = 87 days after hatching], evaluated under the same thermal conditions of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C] that define their active metabolic phase. This attainment of sexual maturity precedes the actual initiation of breeding by a considerable margin, as the species exhibits a delayed first reproduction. Field records from stable colonies indicate that the time since birth at first brood is approximately 1095 days [tR = approximately 1095 days] at the standard metabolic temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], a delay that is typical for many large larids that require several years to acquire the necessary foraging skills and secure a stable nesting territory. This period of adolescence is spent in juvenile and subadult plumage, during which individuals roam widely across the Mediterranean basin. The gap between puberty and first breeding is therefore ecologically significant, representing a phase of skill acquisition and social integration.

The sustained reproductive output of adult Audouin's gulls is constrained by both clutch size and the frequency of nesting attempts. Females typically produce a single clutch of 2 to 3 eggs per breeding attempt [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per breeding attempt], with a modal clutch size of three eggs observed in most years. On average, these breeding adults complete about one clutch annually [F_R_i = about one clutch annually], a frequency that is typical for a long-lived seabird investing in high-quality offspring. Under the prevailing metabolic conditions of breeding adults, maintained at 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C], this rate represents a sustainable upper limit for population growth. The life history strategy is thus one of high adult survival and moderate, but consistent, annual fecundity.

Long-term demographic studies provide a comprehensive picture of the species' lifespan. The maximum recorded longevity for Audouin's gull is approximately 20.9 years [am = approximately 20.9 years], a figure obtained from a long-running banding program in the Ebro Delta and measured under the standard ambient temperature of 40.9 °C [T = 40.9 °C]. This lifespan is noteworthy among Mediterranean seabirds and reflects a life-history strategy heavily weighted toward adult survival, a common pattern in species that face unpredictable food resources. By the time a breeding adult dies from natural senescence, it may have produced dozens of eggs across its reproductive life. The interplay between a modest annual reproductive output and an extended lifespan ensures that population stability is maintained even in years of low breeding success. This demographic profile, with its emphasis on persistence rather than high fecundity, positions the species to better withstand the increasing pressures of habitat degradation, overfishing of its prey base, and climate-induced changes in Mediterranean sea surface temperatures.
